node.label: Caroline Walker Bynum
node.date_label: Jesus as Mother: essay collection (1982) · Holy Feast and Holy Fast (1987) · Fragmentation and Redemption (1991)
node.description: A historian of medieval European religion, gender and the body. Holy Feast and Holy Fast (1987) argues that food lay at the heart of much late-medieval women’s piety: women renounced ordinary food through fasting to prepare for the extraordinary food of the eucharist, and offered themselves as food in miracles of feeding. Where earlier scholars had treated fasting, stigmata and inedia in isolation or through modern medical and psychological theories, she showed how these practices enabled women to exert control within the family and religious life. In ‘Why All the Fuss about the Body?’ (1995) she engages sympathetically with Judith Butler’s performative account of gender, but insists that medieval and modern ideas of body and identity be compared in their own settings; the Middle Ages, she writes, was characterized by ‘a cacophony of discourses’. Jesus as Mother (1982) and Fragmentation and Redemption (1991) are her other major collections on gender and the body in medieval religion.
